title: Evaluating the fake news problem at the scale of the information ecosystem
screen_reason: Passive-metering study of nationally representative US TV, desktop and mobile panels (Nielsen, Comscore) measuring how much of Americans' consumed media diet is fake news, where fake news is defined at publisher/URL level by a list of 98 sites. Reports quantitative shares of consumption with explicit denominators (0.15% of the daily media diet; 1% of news consumption), meeting the EXPOSURE criterion.

estimates.platform: TV plus desktop and mobile web (Nielsen TV panel, Comscore desktop/mobile panel, Nielsen desktop web panel)
estimates.measure_type: % of Americans' total daily media consumption time that is spent on fake news sites
estimates.value_raw: fake news comprises only 0.15% of Americans' daily media diet
estimates.denominator: All daily media consumption by American adults 18+, an average of 460 minutes per person per day across TV, streaming, gaming, social media and desktop/mobile browsing (Nielsen national TV panel N approx. 100,000; Comscore nationally representative desktop and mobile panel; Nielsen desktop web panel 90,000 in 2016 falling to 60,000 in 2018)
estimates.definition: Time spent on 1 of 98 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality or hyperpartisan news (the 'red', 'orange' and 'black' categories), plus imputed passive exposure on social media and search
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Fake news,' broadly defined as false or misleading information masquerading as legitimate news
estimates.n: 460 minutes per person per day of total media consumption (nationally representative US adult panels)
estimates.source_quote: Third, fake news comprises only 0.15% of Americans’ daily media diet.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, p. 1 (restated in Discussion, p. 5: 'our finding that fake news is extremely rare, comprising only about one-tenth of 1% of Americans’ overall daily media diet')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: List of 98 fake news websites assembled by researchers (Grinberg et al. 2019), professional fact checkers and journalists, covering fake/deceptive/low-quality and hyperpartisan sites; classification is at publisher or URL level, except YouTube where a random sample of 360,000 videos (10,000/month, weighted by viewing time) was classified using YouTube's internal 'news and politics' category. No inter-coder reliability applies (list-based classification).
estimates.moderator_quote: fake news consumption is the time spent on 1 of 98 websites previously identified by researchers (8), professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news. Thus, in accordance with the previous literature, with the notable exception of YouTube, fake news is defined at the publisher or URL (Uniform Resource Locator) level.
estimates.notes: Time-weighted diet share, aggregated over the 36 months January 2016 - December 2018; year is given as the 2017 midpoint of that window because the estimate is an aggregate, not a single-year figure. breadth is blank because the numerator is a source-level domain list (and the authors stress it is deliberately broad, including hyperpartisan sites such as Breitbart, so it 'likely overstates the true prevalence').

estimates.platform: TV plus desktop and mobile web (Nielsen TV panel, Comscore desktop/mobile panel, Nielsen desktop web panel)
estimates.measure_type: % of Americans' total news consumption (online plus TV) that is fake news
estimates.value_raw: fake news itself is only 1% of overall news consumption
estimates.denominator: All news consumption by American adults 18+, online and on TV (about 54 minutes of TV news plus 9.7 minutes of online news per person per day; roughly 14.2% of the 460-minute daily media diet)
estimates.definition: Time spent on 1 of 98 websites previously identified by researchers, professional fact checkers and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality or hyperpartisan news, as a share of time spent on news (800+ hard-news websites plus about 400 Nielsen-classified TV news programmes plus portals)
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Fake news,' broadly defined as false or misleading information masquerading as legitimate news
estimates.n: About 64 minutes per person per day of total news consumption (TV 54 min plus online 9.7 min), nationally representative US adult panels
estimates.source_quote: we find that fake news itself is only 1% of overall
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 98-site publisher/URL-level list as the media-diet row; news denominator defined by Nielsen's programme classification for TV (about 400 programmes) and by 800+ hard-news websites plus portals online.
estimates.moderator_quote: Online (mobile and desktop) news consumption is defined as time spent on any article published on one of more than 800 websites, adapted from (21), that primarily cover “hard” news topics like politics, business, and U.S. and international affairs. Correspondingly, fake news consumption is the time spent on 1 of 98 websites previously identified by researchers (8), professional fact checkers, and journalists as sources of fake, deceptive, low-quality, or hyperpartisan news.
estimates.notes: The source_quote is the longest contiguous verbatim span; the PDF's two-column layout breaks the sentence, which reads in full 'Third, whereas the topic of fake news outstrips all other news-related research, we find that fake news itself is only 1% of overall news consumption, substantially lower for Twitter alone (8).' Same underlying measurement as the media-diet row but with the news diet, not total media, as the denominator; it is a distinct estimate rather than a definition variant. Aggregated over January 2016 - December 2018; year given as the 2017 midpoint.

estimates.country: United States (nationally representative US desktop panel)
estimates.measure_type: % of desktop panelists whose fake news consumption exceeded their mainstream news consumption
estimates.value_raw: a very small fraction of desktop panelists (1.97%) did consume more fake news than mainstream news; however, this number drops to 0.7% when restricting to people who consumed at least 1 min of fake news per day. When restricting to just black and red fake news sites (i.e., excluding hyperpartisan sites), these numbers drop to 0.97 and 0.32%
estimates.denominator: Nielsen nationally representative desktop web panelists (90,000 in 2016 decreasing to 60,000 in 2018)
estimates.definition: A panelist whose time on the 98 fake news sites exceeded their time on mainstream news sites over the observation window
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Fake news,' broadly defined as false or misleading information masquerading as legitimate news
estimates.n: Nielsen desktop web panel, 90,000 panelists in 2016 falling to 60,000 in 2018
estimates.source_quote: fraction of desktop panelists (1.97%) did consume more fake news
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 98-site publisher-level list; the stricter variants restrict to the 'black' and 'red' categories, excluding hyperpartisan sites.
estimates.moderator_quote: Because the Nielsen panel records only desktop activity, these figures understate the true consumption of online news (i.e., including mobile).
estimates.notes: The source_quote is the longest contiguous verbatim span; the PDF's two-column layout breaks the sentence, which reads in full 'Of potential concern, a very small fraction of desktop panelists (1.97%) did consume more fake news than mainstream news; however, this number drops to 0.7% when restricting to people who consumed at least 1 min of fake news per day. When restricting to just black and red fake news sites (i.e., excluding hyperpartisan sites), these numbers drop to 0.97 and 0.32%, respectively.' Coded OTHER and flagged borderline: the denominator is people, but the numerator is not 'reached at least once' (which would be REACH) — it is people whose fake-news diet exceeded their mainstream-news diet, a concentration-flavoured statistic that nevertheless does not satisfy the CONCENTRATION rule (no paired top-X% of users / Y% of exposure). Three stricter variants of the same statistic are reported verbatim in the same sentence and are recorded in value_raw rather than as separate rows: 0.7% (restricted to those consuming at least 1 min/day of fake news), 0.97% (black and red sites only) and 0.32% (black and red sites, at least 1 min/day).

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'news consumption ... comprising at most 14.2% of Americans' daily media diets' and 'news accounts for only 4.2% of total online consumption' and 'TV news ... 23% of the total' — shares of news, not of misinformation; (2) '44% of the sample is exposed to no online news at all' — again news, not fake news; (3) 'No age group ... spent more than an average of a minute per day engaging with fake news, nor did it occupy more than 1% of their overall news consumption ... or more than 0.2% of their overall media consumption' — an upper bound across age groups, not a point estimate, and age subgroups are not the paper's headline; (4) the upper- and lower-bound estimates under stricter definitions in fig. S3 and table S10, and the per-age numerical values in table S11 — in the Supplementary Materials, which are not part of this text file. The main measurement caveat the authors themselves raise is that classification is at publisher/URL level, so false content from generally reliable sources is missed and hyperpartisan-but-not-false sites are counted in.

rob.design: Multimode passive metering of nationally representative US panels, January 2016 - December 2018: Nielsen national TV panel (N approx. 100,000, plus a 50,000 subset in the 25 largest local markets), Comscore nationally representative desktop and mobile panel, and Nielsen desktop web panel (90,000 in 2016 decreasing to 60,000 in 2018), with a 15,000-person overlap between the Nielsen web and TV panels. Fake news classified at publisher/URL level from a list of 98 sites compiled by researchers, professional fact-checkers and journalists; news classified from 800+ hard-news domains and about 400 Nielsen-classified TV news programmes; YouTube handled by classifying a random sample of 360,000 videos weighted by viewing time. No response rate or inter-coder reliability reported (list-based, behavioural measurement). Data at https://osf.io/cygta/.
rob.item6_quote: “Fake news,” broadly defined as false or misleading information masquerading as legitimate news, is frequently asserted to be pervasive online with serious consequences for democracy.
rob.item10_quote: Of the 460 min per person per day of total media consumption, approximately 400 min (86%) is not related to news of any kind (see table S6 for exact figures).
